tldr: Policies learned in simulation often fail on real humanoid hardware because of the actuator sim-to-real gap. Contact-UAN solves this by learning an actuator residual model unsupervised from just 6.5 minutes of real walking data. By inferring the stance-foot contact state from onboard proprioception to align simulator replay, it enables dynamic jumps and compliant force control while reducing running torque by 20% and force-tracking error by 43%.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of Contact-UAN. a) From proprioceptive data recorded on hardware, the system estimates contact state and velocity, then replays rollouts in simulation with consistent contact forces to train the UAN (residual model). b) Downstream task policies are trained in the simulation environment augmented with the trained UAN. c) During hardware deployment, only the task policy is executed, adding zero inference overhead.
overview:
When you train a humanoid robot with reinforcement learning in simulation, you often get policies that look great, walking and running cleanly. However, once deployed on hardware, motors frequently overheat and shut down, or the robot fails to absorb landing impacts and falls over. At the heart of this problem lies the discrepancy between simulated actuator dynamics (motors and gearboxes) and real hardware. Especially in tasks involving environmental force interactions, small errors in joint torque lead directly to failures in regulating ground reaction forces and external loads.

To tackle this, the authors focus on a residual world model approach. It preserves the simulator's accurate physics priors for rigid-body dynamics and contact modeling, while using a neural network to correct discrepancies in actuator commands. But when trying to replay recorded hardware trajectories in simulation to learn these errors unsupervised, you hit a major roadblock. In penalty-based soft contact models, a mismatch of just a couple of millimeters in foot penetration depth or a few degrees in tilt causes massive shifts in ground reaction forces. If replay initialization lacks contact consistency, the residual network mistakenly learns to compensate for reset artifacts instead of true actuator errors.

Contact-UAN resolves this by inferring the simulator-side stance-foot penetration depth and orientation needed to reproduce real-world contact wrenches, using only onboard proprioception such as joint positions and IMU signals. This allows replay to start with fully aligned contact forces. In experiments on the Unitree G1 humanoid, a correction model trained on just 6.5 minutes of random walking data reduced running torque by 20%, cut end-effector force-tracking error by 43%, and enabled dynamic, high jumps that reliably absorb heavy landing impacts.
contributions: Established a framework for contact-consistent replay initialization that infers the simulator-side stance-foot pose (penetration depth and tilt) from onboard proprioception alone.

Introduced a residual model that corrects actuator command discrepancies while preserving the physics engine and contact solver, enabling highly accurate sim-to-real environments without joint torque sensors.

Demonstrated seamless real-world transfer across diverse force-dependent tasks using a single model trained on just 6.5 minutes of walking data, achieving a 20% torque reduction in running, a 43% lower force-tracking error, compliant impedance control, and robust high jumps.

sections.heading: Why do contact interactions make simulation gaps so severe for humanoids?
sections.summary: Sim-to-real transfer requires more than matching visual kinematics; force profiles that dictate efficiency and impact absorption must match as well. Given the limitations of domain randomization and fully learned world models, this work proposes Contact-UAN, which learns actuator residuals via contact-consistent replay.
sections.details:
In reinforcement learning for humanoid robots, policies transferred directly from simulation to hardware often look fine kinematically, yet fail to exert the intended forces when pushing against the ground or absorbing external loads. This happens because analytical simulators oversimplify complex motor dynamics like nonlinear friction, torque saturation, and gearbox backlash.

To bridge this actuator sim-to-real gap, domain randomization (DR) is commonly used. However, randomizing parameters across wide ranges often yields overly conservative policies that fail to leverage the hardware's full capability. Conversely, fully learned world models that learn environmental dynamics from scratch require massive datasets and risk reward hacking by drifting from physical laws. A compelling middle ground is residual learning: keep the simulator's solid physics structure (rigid-body dynamics and contact solvers) intact, and use a neural network to correct only the discrepancies in the actuator command channel.

However, because many humanoids lack joint torque sensors, residual learning must rely on replaying hardware joint trajectories in simulation to minimize tracking error. This brings up a critical obstacle: contact initialization. In simulator contact models (such as penalty methods), a few millimeters of foot penetration or a couple of degrees of tilt can halve or double the resulting forces and moments. If replay starts with misaligned contact forces, the residual model ends up learning to cancel out reset artifacts instead of true actuator differences. Contact-UAN solves this contact-consistent initialization using only onboard sensors, successfully isolating and learning the true actuator discrepancies.

captions.F3: Sensitivity of contact wrenches (forces and moments) to initial pose. In the MuJoCo model, a foot penetration error of just 2 mm reduces vertical reaction force by about 50%, and a 2-degree foot pitch error changes supporting pitch torque by around 45%. This extreme sensitivity makes contact-consistent resets indispensable for replay learning.

sections.heading: Method: Inferring contact pose from proprioception to train the residual model
sections.summary: Contact-UAN operates in three stages. First, it infers the stance-foot pose and velocity needed to reproduce contact from proprioceptive history. Next, it replays hardware rollouts to train the actuator correction network (UAN) via PPO. Finally, task policies are trained inside the corrected simulator.
sections.details:
### 2.1 Contact-Consistent Replay Initialization
When replaying hardware trajectories in simulation, directly measuring floating-base positions and contact forces without external motion capture is extremely difficult. The authors train an estimator that uses a short history of onboard proprioception (3 steps, 60 ms)—such as loaded joint responses and IMU readings—to infer the simulator-side stance-foot penetration depth and tilt required to reproduce hardware contact forces.

Two design choices are crucial here. First, including swing feet during training leads to large errors, so a contact classifier first identifies the stance foot, and pose regression is applied only to feet in contact. Second, floating-base height is deliberately excluded from observations, forcing the model to estimate penetration from load-induced deformation cues rather than simple position matching. When both feet touch the ground, base heights inferred from each foot are fused smoothly using contact probabilities.

### 2.2 UAN as a Residual World Model
The UAN learns the dynamic discrepancy between hardware and simulation as an additive offset $\delta q_t$ to joint position targets. Retaining the simulator's physics engine and PD controllers, the policy's target angles $q^{\text{base}}_t$ are modified by adding $\delta q_t$ before being passed to the simulator. Inputs to the UAN are limited to joint target tracking errors and joint velocity histories (60 ms) to prevent overfitting. Furthermore, MLP parameters are shared across identical motor models on the robot to maximize data efficiency. Training uses PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization) with a reward that minimizes mean squared error in joint positions and velocities between hardware and simulation.

### 2.3 Policy Training and Deployment
Once trained, the UAN weights are frozen and embedded directly into the simulation environment. Downstream task policies, such as running or jumping, are then trained via RL in this corrected simulator. Importantly, domain randomization over internal robot parameters is completely removed. During deployment, the UAN remains inside the simulator and is not placed on the robot; only the learned task policy is executed, adding zero runtime overhead.

captions.F4: Overall method workflow. a) Contact states are inferred from offline hardware proprioception, simulator replay is initialized with consistent contact, and the UAN is trained via RL. b) Task policies are trained inside the simulation corrected by the frozen UAN. c) At deployment, only the task policy runs on hardware, adding no extra computational cost or inference overhead.

sections.heading: Experimental setup: Verification tasks and testbed with the Unitree G1
sections.summary: The method is evaluated on the 29-DoF Unitree G1 humanoid using baseline parameters from BeyondMimic. Trained on only 6.5 minutes of real walking data, UAN is tested across three force-critical downstream tasks: running, force regulation, and jumping.
sections.details:
### Hardware and Simulator Setup
Experiments were conducted on the Unitree G1, a 29-DoF humanoid. The nominal simulation environment uses the MuJoCo-based model (mjlab) provided by the recent BeyondMimic baseline. It relies on manufacturer-provided inertia values and nominal PD gains, with no prior dedicated system identification (SysID) performed before training Contact-UAN.

### Data Collection and Downstream Tasks
Hardware training data for the UAN was gathered using a Walk-These-Ways (WTW) style locomotion policy trained with domain randomization in the nominal simulator. By varying stepping frequency and foot swing height, only 6.5 minutes of proprioceptive data were recorded, capturing diverse impact velocities and ground contact durations.

Three downstream tasks demanding precise force generation and impact absorption were evaluated:
- **Running**: Requires efficient ground force generation, tested up to commanded speeds of 3.0 m/s.
- **Force & Impedance Control**: Requires exerting downward forces up to 50 N through an elastic band attached to the hand. Passive compliance and Cartesian position impedance control were also evaluated.
- **Jumping**: Demands large propulsive impulses at takeoff and heavy impact absorption during landing.

In addition to hardware tests, the authors built "Sim-to-Sim" environments with varying severity (easy, medium, hard) by perturbing damping, friction, latency, and encoder biases to thoroughly evaluate robustness under severe model mismatches.

sections.heading: Results: 20% lower torque consumption, reliable jumps, and precise force control
sections.summary: Contact-UAN cut joint torque mismatch by roughly 69% and reduced running torque by 20% on hardware while matching speed. Force-tracking error dropped by 43%, and high-jump policies landed stably even after aggressive reward tuning that caused the baseline to crash.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Residual Model Accuracy and Contact Initialization Effects
Evaluating the stance-foot pose estimator revealed that training only on the stance phase reduced root mean squared error (RMSE) in contact height by an order of magnitude compared to naive training over the entire gait cycle. In replay tests using hardware running data, Contact-UAN reduced the cumulative joint torque discrepancy between the nominal simulator and hardware by 69.2%. Furthermore, when provided with oracle initial states, enabling UAN dropped joint position RMSE from 0.0720 rad to 0.0184 rad, confirming that the UAN learns genuine actuator dynamics rather than simply masking reset errors.

### 4.2 Sim-to-Real Transfer on Hardware Tasks
- **Fast Running**: Across commanded speeds from 1.0 to 2.5 m/s, the UAN-based policy matched baseline ground speeds while cutting torque usage by 20%. Because unnecessary torque output was eliminated, the UAN policy easily completed an intense 3.0 m/s test (measured at 3.13 m/s), whereas the baseline triggered motor thermal protection and shut down.
- **Accurate Force and Impedance Control**: In external force tracking tests using a spring scale, overall tracking error dropped by 42.8% compared to the baseline. Improvements were especially striking under heavy loads (large downward forces) where deep knee flexion and whole-body bracing are required. With a zero-force command, the robot exhibited extreme passive compliance, smoothly following external tugs on its arm, and successfully performed sensorless circular impedance control using only proprioception.
- **Dynamic Jumping**: Both policies succeeded when merely tracking a kinematic reference jump. However, once fine-tuned with rewards to maximize jump height, a stark difference emerged. The baseline policy exploited inaccurate simulator actuator limits and failed to brace properly upon landing, falling over on hardware. In contrast, the UAN policy transferred without issue, achieving higher jumps and landing stably while absorbing push disturbances.

### 4.3 Sim-to-Sim Verification
In the "hard" Sim-to-Sim environment with extreme actuator mismatches, the UAN policy with contact-consistent resets achieved a 96.7% 20-second survival rate (dropping to 49.8% with direct unaligned resets). Additionally, supplementing 5 minutes of walking data with 5 minutes of running data showed minimal performance difference, proving that short low-speed walking data generalizes broadly across diverse dynamic motions.

sections.heading: Limitations: Inter-joint coupling and thermal drift remain unaddressed
sections.summary: Because Contact-UAN models each actuator independently, it currently cannot account for cross-joint coupling effects or changes in motor properties caused by heat buildup over prolonged operation.
sections.details:
While Contact-UAN achieves strong practical results, several limitations remain.

- **Unmodeled Multi-Joint Coupling**: To maximize data efficiency, UAN assigns independent MLPs to each motor type. As a result, it cannot capture coupling effects between joints caused by wiring voltage drops, shared power bus limits, or structural frame compliance. Addressing this will likely require cross-attention mechanisms or whole-body network architectures.
- **Motor Temperature-Dependent Variations**: Motor winding resistance and torque constants drift slowly as heat builds up during extended operation. Identifying these long-timescale thermal dynamics from a brief 6.5-minute dataset is difficult. Explicitly incorporating thermal models or integrating temperature sensor feedback remains future work.

sections.heading: Related work: Positioning against SysID, domain randomization, and world models
sections.summary: Unlike conservative domain randomization or data-hungry fully learned world models, this work adopts a residual world model framework that preserves rigid-body physics while correcting only actuator discrepancies.
sections.details:
### System Identification (SysID) and Domain Randomization (DR)
Conventional sim-to-real pipelines typically identify rigid-body parameters via analytical models or inject broad parameter variations via DR to foster robustness. However, DR often produces over-cautious policies that fail to push hardware to its physical limits. While recent efforts aim to reduce DR through higher-fidelity models, this work avoids tedious manual modeling of complex gear friction by absorbing discrepancies into a neural network residual.

### Robot World Models
Fully learned world models that replace the entire physics engine with deep neural networks (such as RWM or DayDreamer) remove rigid-body modeling assumptions. However, they require tens of hours of real data and often suffer from reward hacking when policies exploit model prediction errors. Contact-UAN avoids this by preserving the simulator's rigid-body equations and contact solvers, preventing unphysical drift and enabling stable RL with just minutes of data.

### Actuator Networks and Residual Learning
Prior work learning actuator input-output relationships (such as Supervised Actuator Networks) generally required ground-truth torque sensor data. While unsupervised replay approaches (such as UAN or ASAP) have been explored, they were confined to floating manipulators or required external motion capture setups. Contact-UAN is the first to combine proprioceptive contact inference with residual replay learning to achieve unsupervised actuator identification for whole-body, contact-rich legged humanoids without torque sensors or cameras.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Combining physics simulators with data for efficient humanoid control
sections.summary: Contact-UAN demonstrates that aligning contact states from onboard proprioception enables high-precision actuator residual modeling on torque-sensorless humanoids. Blending physics priors with data-driven corrections offers a remarkably efficient path forward.
sections.details:
This paper introduced Contact-UAN, a residual world model designed to bridge the actuator-level sim-to-real gap for humanoid robots.

By establishing an initialization pipeline that infers stance-foot penetration and tilt from onboard proprioception to align simulator contact forces with hardware, the approach completely prevents replay learning from being corrupted by reset artifacts. Consequently, with only 6.5 minutes of regular walking data, the method unlocked wide-ranging capabilities: a 20% torque reduction during running, a 43% lower force-tracking error, and successful high-impact hardware jumps.

Leveraging the generalization and reliability of rigid-body physics engines while smartly correcting the most problematic actuator gap with real-world data, this strategy stands out as a highly effective blueprint for balancing data efficiency and dynamic performance in whole-body humanoid control.

sections.heading: Appendix: State estimator details and comparison with fully learned world models
sections.summary: The appendix details the network architecture and formulations for the contact classifier and foot pose estimator, PPO training hyperparameters, and the massive data-efficiency advantage (over 400x) of Contact-UAN compared to fully learned world models (RWM-U).
sections.details:
### State Estimation and Contact-Weighted Fusion (Appendix A)
To reconstruct contact conditions in simulation, separate MLPs estimate contact probability $\hat{p}_{i,t}$, relative height $\hat{h}_{i,t}$, and foot-frame gravity vector $\hat{g}^{F_i}_{i,t}$ for each foot. Only feet whose contact probability exceeds a threshold (0.8) are retained, and base height along with roll and pitch orientations are recovered via forward kinematics (FK). When both feet are grounded, base states are smoothly blended using a weighted average based on contact probabilities.

### Comparison with Fully Learned World Models (Appendix F)
An offline fully learned world model, RWM-U, was optimized for the G1 humanoid and compared head-to-head against Contact-UAN. Even when trained on 33 hours (around 6 million steps) of hardware data, policies trained inside RWM-U achieved a maximum survival rate of only 38.2% in the target environment. In contrast, Contact-UAN reached a 100% expert-level survival rate with only 5 minutes of data—over 400 times less data. This quantitatively proves the immense benefit of retaining rigid-body physics priors instead of learning world dynamics from scratch.

### Sensor Noise and Ablations (Appendix G)
Even under harsh sensor degradations—such as adding a constant 2-degree pitch bias to the IMU or applying a 5 Hz low-pass filter (introducing latency) to joint velocities—Contact-UAN maintained a 20-second survival rate above 97%. Ablations also compared the position-residual formulation against torque residuals and direct supervised torque prediction, showing comparable downstream performance. This demonstrates that adding residuals to position commands is the simplest and most effective strategy for humanoids that lack reliable torque sensing on hardware.

takeaways: In contact-rich replay learning, tiny contact mismatches (millimeters of penetration or degrees of tilt) ruin training because models compensate for reset artifacts; contact-consistent initialization is vital.

Instead of replacing the simulator with deep learning, retaining rigid-body physics and learning only actuator command residuals yields overwhelming advantages in both data efficiency (minutes of data) and physical consistency.
Even on standard humanoids lacking joint torque sensors, high-fidelity unsupervised actuator identification is achievable by inferring contact states from short histories of onboard proprioception.
limitations: Inter-actuator electrical and structural coupling effects cannot be modeled because actuators are represented by independent MLP networks.
Thermal drift—such as reduced torque capacity and changing winding resistance caused by motor heating during prolonged operation—cannot be captured from short datasets.
The contact estimator is trained on simulation data assuming flat terrain, so extending it to extreme rough terrain or staircases will require further adaptations.
